column3: It closely repeats the ritual of naming God over livestock He provided, the central action in the focus.
Its warning against invoking powerless others does not develop pilgrimage, livestock provision, or feeding the poor.
God's witnessing of deeds offers only a broad counterpart to the participants witnessing benefits in the focus.
It directly continues the sacrifice sequence: name God over the animals, eat from them, and feed those in need.
God's witness over all communities supplies the surah's wider witnessing frame, though not the focus's ritual meal.
The naming of a future messenger does not clarify naming God over provision or the Hajj practice.
It provides a direct corrective contrast: people falsely restrict livestock and omit God's name over them.
The preparation of the House for worshipers establishes the sacred destination and worship setting that leads into the focus.
The unique name given to Yahya is unrelated to ritual naming, provision, or feeding.
It joins eating permitted food with naming God over it, closely paralleling the focus's named provision and command to eat.
Those who spend from what God provided extend the focus's movement from received provision toward sharing it.
It clarifies that provision and feeding do not flow to God from people, supporting the focus's God-given direction of food.
It condemns forbidding provision God supplied, a substantive contrast to receiving livestock as lawful provision in the focus.
Benefit from truthfulness on the Day of Judgment does not develop the focus's witnessed benefits or shared meal.
Its bare witness-and-witnessed formula only lightly echoes the focus's language of witnessing benefits.
It explicitly connects God-given provision with spending it, supporting the focus's distribution of provision to the poor.
Its assigned witness-bearing role completes the surah's witnessing theme and retains the Abrahamic communal setting of the Hajj passage.
God's guarantee of every creature's provision broadly supports the source of provision, without the focus's livestock or sharing practice.
It directly names the Hajj and its known months, closely framing the focus's specified days and pilgrimage setting.
The immediately preceding call brings people to Hajj, whose purpose and food practice are stated in the focus.
Spending from what God provided gives a general parallel to turning received provision outward to others.
It commands eating what God's name has been mentioned over, directly paralleling the focus's named livestock and eating command.
The alternation of night and day and God's hearing and sight do not clarify the focus's ritual provision.
The prohibition on derisive labels concerns human social speech rather than naming God over food.
It identifies livestock as lawful while pilgrims are in consecration, providing a relevant legal setting for the focus's animal provision.
Permitted intercession does not develop the focus's benefits, sacrifice, or feeding.
Glorifying the Lord's name gives a limited verbal parallel to the focus's command to mention God's name.
Its counted days and feeding of a needy person form a useful ritual parallel, though it concerns fasting rather than Hajj livestock.
It immediately continues the Hajj sequence with completing rites, fulfilling vows, and circling the ancient House.
Provision of good things and gratitude broadly support receiving divine provision, without the focus's ritual distribution.
It explicitly joins livestock, many benefits, and eating from them, closely matching the focus's animal provision and consumption.
The appointed worship rite for each community parallels the focus's communal Hajj observance, without its food details.
The repeated command to glorify the Lord's name is only a general counterpart to naming God over livestock.
It presents livestock as made for human use and eating, supporting the focus's treatment of livestock as provided food.
The contrast between powerless objects and God does not illuminate the focus's sacrificial meal or distribution.
Feeding sixty needy people provides a concrete parallel to the focus's command to feed the distressed poor.
It names benefits from the sacrificial animals and their destination at the ancient House, directly preparing the focus's scene.
Rain making the earth green does not clarify the focus's livestock rite or feeding command.
It preserves places where God's name is often mentioned, offering only a broader worship-setting parallel.
It challenges those favored in provision who refuse to share it with dependents, reinforcing the focus's outward distribution of provision.
Joseph's lodging and anticipated benefit do not develop the focus's pilgrimage or food-sharing practice.
Standing by testimony only faintly echoes the focus's witnessing language, without its ritual context.
Witnessing a specified month and magnifying God provide a calendar-and-remembrance parallel, though this is Ramadan rather than Hajj.
The ruined town imagery does not clarify witnessed benefits, livestock, or feeding.
Witnesses over revealed law give a broad testimony parallel, but not the focus's pilgrimage meal.
It explicitly gives livestock benefits and drinks and calls for gratitude, closely supporting the focus's benefits from animal provision.
The demand for a promised judgment does not develop the focus's ritual benefits or food distribution.
God, the messenger, and believers seeing deeds offers only a general witnessing parallel to the focus.
Its invented exclusions around livestock food form a relevant contrast to the focus's open command to eat and feed from God's provision.
Turning away from rejecters does not clarify the focus's provision or ritual practice.
The formula beginning in God's name provides a direct but contextually limited parallel to mentioning His name.
The command to enter humbly and eat plentifully offers a distant worship-and-provision parallel.
The usefulness of reminder for believers does not develop the focus's witnessed benefits or meal.
God's witness over everything only broadly overlaps the focus's language of witnessing.
Belief becoming useless after punishment does not clarify the focus's benefits or feeding.
The testing of towns through hardship does not develop the focus's sacred provision.
God and knowledgeable beings witnessing divine unity is a broad testimony parallel, without the focus's ritual action.
It identifies benefits from livestock and their service to human needs, supporting one element of the focus's animal provision.
The Book's descent does not clarify the focus's pilgrimage food practice.
Cosmic creation and celestial regulation do not develop the focus's named livestock provision.
Alliance with disbelievers and divine anger do not clarify the focus's ritual or sharing command.
A town's belief becoming beneficial concerns deliverance, not the focus's witnessed benefits or provision.
A messenger as witness supplies only a general testimony parallel to the focus's witnessing language.
God's comprehensive knowledge of creation and human deeds does not clarify the focus's Hajj meal.
The failure of other gods to help does not develop the focus's provision or feeding.
The naming of a Paradise spring is unrelated to naming God over livestock.
It regulates rightful eating from entrusted wealth and requires witnesses for transfer, but does not develop the focus's communal feeding.
The absence of intercessors does not clarify the focus's benefits or food distribution.
Teaching Adam the names is only a distant lexical parallel to the focus's mention of God's name.
Provision in Paradise broadly echoes divine provision, without the focus's animal meal or needy recipients.
The absence of a close friend does not develop the focus's ritual provision.
Good provision for believers offers a general parallel, but no Hajj, livestock, or feeding detail.
It explicitly requires feeding needy people from the ordinary food one provides, closely paralleling the focus's feeding command.
The replacement of hardship with ease does not clarify the focus's provision or ritual practice.
Remembering the Lord's name at set times gives a limited parallel to the focus's naming in specified days.
The command to eat lawful, good gain is a general food parallel, without ritual naming or care for the poor.
It states that livestock are subdued for human use and eaten, directly supporting the focus's provided animal food.
Provision for martyrs with their Lord is a general provision parallel, not a shared earthly meal.
Creation and the lack of protectors or intercessors do not clarify the focus's ritual food practice.
The failure of wealth and children on Judgment Day does not develop the focus's benefits or feeding.
God's beautiful names provide only a broad background for mentioning His name in the focus.
The judgment of those who refuse their Lord does not clarify the focus's animal provision or sharing.
Transport upon livestock supplies one practical benefit that complements the focus's benefits from them.
God's beautiful names and universal praise offer only a general naming-and-glorification parallel.
The harm and benefit of false patrons do not develop the focus's witnessed benefits or provision.
Eating as heedless worldly enjoyment contrasts only superficially and does not clarify the focus's commanded meal.
The phrase about present sons does not develop the focus's witnessing, provision, or feeding.
Giving charity to the poor directly parallels the focus's command to feed the distressed and needy.
Noah's counsel and divine misguidance do not clarify the focus's ritual provision.
Naming things accompanies divine knowledge, but it does not develop naming God over provision.
Human creation and rain-revived earth do not clarify the focus's Hajj food sequence.
Reading in the Creator's name provides a general parallel to invoking God's name, without the focus's provision context.
The arrogance of Ad and denial of signs do not develop the focus's ritual or feeding practice.
God's witnessing of all recitation and action is only a broad counterpart to participants witnessing benefits.
Obeying the messenger and his duty of delivery do not clarify the focus's food distribution.
It commands eating the good provision God gave while setting limits on misuse, supporting the focus's reception of divine food.
The battlefield account and hidden thoughts do not develop the focus's ritual benefits or meal.
God's witness over deeds offers only a general testimony parallel to the focus's witnessing language.
Noah's blessing and later punishment of communities do not clarify the focus's provision or feeding.
Spending from what God provided supports the focus's movement from received provision toward helping others.
It places Safa and Marwah among God's rites for Hajj and Umrah, supplying a direct pilgrimage-rite setting for the focus.
It commands believers to eat the good things God provided and thank Him, supporting the focus's reception of provision as divine gift.
It makes giving wealth to relatives, orphans, and the needy part of righteousness, extending the focus's care for the poor.
It joins completion of Hajj, sacrificial offerings, and expiatory feeding, making it a major omitted parallel to the focus's ritual food practice.
It explicitly situates seeking God's bounty within Hajj, directly clarifying the focus's witnessed benefits in the pilgrimage setting.
It commands remembrance of God after completing the Hajj rites, supporting the focus's remembrance within those rites.
It commands remembrance of God during numbered days, closely paralleling the focus's specified days and naming of God.
It identifies parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy as recipients of spending, supporting the focus's outward distribution to the poor.
It commands spending from what God provided, a general but clear parallel to provision being passed onward.
It requires spending from good things people have earned and God has produced, supporting the focus's ethic of sharing received provision.
It identifies poor people unable to travel or solicit, closely resonating with the focus's concern for the distressed poor.
It establishes pilgrimage to the House as a duty, directly supplying the larger obligation in which the focus's practice occurs.
It requires giving relatives, orphans, and the needy something when wealth is divided, paralleling the focus's inclusion of poor recipients.
It expressly names God's rites, the sacred month, and sacrificial animals, directly framing the focus's Hajj livestock practice.
It commands eating the lawful and good provision God supplied, supporting the focus's lawful consumption of divine provision.
Its Hajj-related expiation can take the form of an offering reaching the Kaaba or feeding needy people, tightly joining the focus's two concerns.
It identifies the Kaaba, sacred month, sacrificial animals, and garlanded offerings as supports for communal order, directly contextualizing the focus.
It asks why people would not eat what God's name has been mentioned over, closely matching the focus's named provision and eating command.
It prohibits eating that over which God's name was not mentioned, the direct negative counterpart to the focus's ritual naming.
It names livestock as provision and commands eating what God provided, closely supporting the focus's livestock meal.
Providing water for pilgrims and maintaining the sacred mosque give a related service-to-pilgrims context for the focus's Hajj gathering.
It assigns alms to poor and needy recipients, extending the focus's concrete concern for the distressed poor.
It explicitly states that livestock provide warmth, benefits, and food, closely matching the focus's benefits from and eating of livestock.
It presents livestock as a source of nourishing drink, supporting the focus's broader treatment of animals as God-given provision.
It commands eating the lawful and good provision God gave and giving thanks, directly supporting the focus's consumption of divine provision.
It commands giving the needy their due, supplying a direct ethical parallel to feeding the distressed poor.
Its command to eat and pasture livestock offers a limited animal-provision parallel without the focus's ritual naming or poor recipients.
It concerns access to the sacred mosque for resident and visiting worshipers, reinforcing the pilgrimage destination presupposed by the focus.
It calls for honoring God's rites, supplying the immediate sacred-rite frame for the focus's named animal provision.
It clarifies that neither sacrificial flesh nor blood reaches God, while the animals are subjected so people magnify Him, directly completing the focus's sacrifice logic.
It commands people of means to give to relatives, the needy, and migrants, extending the focus's distribution of provision.
It directs people to give the needy and traveler their due, directly supporting the focus's care for the poor.
It records the command to spend from what God has provided, directly expressing the transfer of received provision toward those in need.
It introduces livestock as divinely created and placed under human possession, forming the immediate basis for the eating and benefits in the following verses.
It assigns a known share of wealth to the petitioner and deprived person, closely paralleling the focus's required inclusion of the poor.
It requires that distributed wealth not remain only among the rich, supporting the focus's outward circulation of provision.
Failure to urge feeding the poor is treated as culpable, supplying a direct negative counterpart to the focus's feeding command.
It identifies a recognized right within believers' wealth, preparing the recipient-specific distribution stated in the next ayah.
It assigns that recognized right to the petitioner and deprived person, closely paralleling the focus's concern for the distressed poor.
The condemned admit they did not feed the poor, providing a direct negative counterpart to the focus's command.
It explicitly describes giving food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving it, directly paralleling the focus's food distribution.
Failure to urge feeding the poor is condemned, furnishing a direct negative counterpart to the focus's command.
Feeding on a day of severe hunger is a direct parallel to the focus's command to feed a person in need.
It specifies an impoverished person lying in dust as a recipient of food, closely matching the focus's distressed poor.
Failure to encourage feeding the poor is identified as a defining religious failure, directly contrasting the focus's command.
